{{Short description|Bijection of a set using properties of shapes in space}}
{{broader|Transformation (mathematics)}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''geometric transformation''' is any [[bijection]] of a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] to itself (or to another such set) with some salient [[geometry|geometrical]] underpinning, such as preserving distances, [[angle]]s, or ratios (scale). More specifically, it is a [[function (mathematics)|function]] whose [[Domain of a function|domain]] and [[Range of a function|range]] are sets of [[point (geometry)|points]] – most often a [[real coordinate space]], <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math> or <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math> – such that the function is bijective so that its [[Inverse function|inverse]] exists.<ref name="Usiskin-2003">{{cite book | last1=Usiskin | first1=Zalman | author-link1= Zalman Usiskin | first2=Anthony L. | last2=Peressini | first3 = Elena | last3 = Marchisotto |author-link3 = Elena Marchisotto  | first4 = Dick | last4 = Stanley 
| title=Mathematics for High School Teachers: An Advanced Perspective | publisher = Pearson Education | date=2003 | isbn=0-13-044941-5 | oclc=50004269 | page= 84}}</ref> The study of geometry may be approached by the study of these transformations, such as in [[transformation geometry]].<ref>{{citation|first=Gerard A.|last=Venema|title=Foundations of Geometry|year=2006|publisher=[[Pearson Prentice Hall]]|isbn=9780131437005|page=285}}</ref>

==Classifications==
Geometric transformations can be classified by the dimension of their operand sets (thus distinguishing between, say, planar transformations and spatial transformations). They can also be classified according to the properties they preserve:
* [[Displacement (vector)|Displacement]]s preserve [[distance]]s and [[angle|oriented angles]] (e.g., [[Translation (geometry)|translations]]);<ref>{{Cite web|title=Geometry Translation|url=https://www.mathsisfun.com/geometry/translation.html|website=www.mathsisfun.com|access-date=2020-05-02}}</ref>
* [[Isometry|Isometries]] preserve angles and distances (e.g., [[Euclidean transformation]]s);<ref>{{Cite web|title=Geometric Transformations — Euclidean Transformations|url=https://pages.mtu.edu/~shene/COURSES/cs3621/NOTES/geometry/geo-tran.html#euclidean|website=pages.mtu.edu|access-date=2020-05-02}}</ref><ref name=Berger>{{google books |id=pN0iAVavPR8C|page=131}}</ref>
* [[Similarity (geometry)|Similarities]] preserve angles and ratios between distances (e.g., resizing);<ref>{{Cite web|title=Transformations|url=https://www.mathsisfun.com/geometry/transformations.html|website=www.mathsisfun.com|access-date=2020-05-02}}</ref>
* [[Affine transformation]]s preserve [[parallel (geometry)|parallelism]] (e.g., [[Scaling (geometry)|scaling]], [[Shear mapping|shear]]);<ref name=Berger /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Geometric Transformations — Affine Transformations|url=https://pages.mtu.edu/~shene/COURSES/cs3621/NOTES/geometry/geo-tran.html#affine|website=pages.mtu.edu|access-date=2020-05-02}}</ref>
* [[Projective transformation]]s preserve [[collinearity]];<ref name=Wilkinson>Leland Wilkinson, D. Wills, D. Rope, A. Norton, R. Dubbs – ''{{google books|id=NRyGnjeNKJIC|page=182}}''</ref>

Each of these classes contains the previous one.<ref name=Wilkinson />

*[[Möbius transformation]]s using complex coordinates on the plane (as well as [[circle inversion]]) preserve the set of all lines and circles, but may interchange lines and circles.

<gallery>
France identique.gif | Original image (based on the map of France)
France par rotation 180deg.gif | [[Isometry]]
France par similitude.gif | [[similarity (geometry)|Similarity]]

* [[Conformal transformation]]s preserve angles, and are, in the first order, similarities.
* [[Equiareal map|Equiareal transformations]], preserve areas in the planar case or volumes in the three dimensional case.<ref>{{google books|id=Y6jDAgAAQBAJ|page=191}} Bruce E. Meserve – Fundamental Concepts of Geometry, page 191.]</ref> and are, in the first order, affine transformations of [[determinant]] 1.
*[[Homeomorphism]]s (bicontinuous transformations) preserve the neighborhoods of points.
* [[Diffeomorphism]]s (bidifferentiable transformations) are the transformations that are affine in the first order; they contain the preceding ones as special cases, and can be further refined.

Transformations of the same type form [[Group (mathematics)|groups]] that may be sub-groups of other transformation groups.

==Opposite group actions==
{{main|Group action|Opposite group}}
Many geometric transformations are expressed with linear algebra. The bijective linear transformations are elements of a [[general linear group]]. The [[linear transformation]] ''A'' is non-singular. For a [[row vector]] ''v'', the [[matrix product]] ''vA'' gives another row vector ''w'' = ''vA''.

The [[transpose]] of a row vector ''v'' is a column vector ''v''<sup>T</sup>, and the transpose of the above equality is <math>w^T = (vA)^T = A^T v^T .</math> Here ''A''<sup>T</sup> provides a left action  on column vectors.

In transformation geometry there are [[composition of relations|compositions]] ''AB''. Starting with a row vector ''v'', the right action of the composed transformation is ''w'' = ''vAB''. After transposition, 
<math display="block">w^T = (vAB)^T = (AB)^Tv^T = B^T A^T v^T .</math>
Thus for ''AB'' the associated left [[group action]] is <math>B^T A^T .</math> In the study of [[opposite group]]s, the distinction is made between opposite group actions because [[commutative group]]s are the only groups for which these opposites are equal.
